claims.claim: Didymus the Blind was a Christian theologian who headed the influential catechetical school of Alexandria and lived circa 313–398 in Alexandria.
He lost his eyesight at about four years old, remained a layman, and became a leading ascetic scholar and disciple of Origen.

In 386 Jerome visited Alexandria and asked Didymus to write a commentary on the Prophet Zechariah because Origen’s own commentary stopped at chapter five and Zechariah was regarded as the longest and most obscure of the Minor Prophets.
Didymus composed the Zechariah commentary shortly after Jerome’s request, probably in 387, and delivered the work to Jerome by 393.

Didymus’s allegorical method reflects his Origenist background, and his works were later condemned for Origenist tendencies at the Second Council of Constantinople (553), which led to the loss of most of his writings.
The Zechariah commentary survived in a single papyrus codex discovered in 1941 at the monastic site of Tura (Toura) near Cairo, a manuscript copied in the late 6th or early 7th century.

It is the only complete Greek commentary by Didymus whose authenticity is established, transmitted directly in manuscript rather than through catenae, and it has been critically edited, making it uniquely valuable for studying early Alexandrian exegesis.
